title: Views and Indexes
summary: A view saves a query under a name. An index helps the database find certain rows more quickly.
introduction: A view saves a query under a name. An index helps the database find certain rows more quickly. A saved reading list and a book index have different jobs. Learn which tool helps you reuse a question and which helps find an answer.
learningObjectives: Explain what a view stores and what it does not
Create indexes and confirm their use with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
Decide which columns deserve an index

blocks.text: `CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...` stores the query. Afterwards the view can be used in FROM like a table: filtered, sorted and joined. The three-table join from the JOIN lesson becomes a one-line query:

blocks.code:
CREATE VIEW order_details AS
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, o.quantity,
       ROUND(p.price * o.quantity, 2) AS line_total, o.ordered_on
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id;
SELECT customer, product, line_total
FROM order_details
WHERE line_total > 30
ORDER BY line_total DESC;

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE VIEW order_details AS

customer         | product             | line_total
-----------------+---------------------+-----------
Ada Lovelace     | Mechanical keyboard | 89
Guido van Rossum | Mechanical keyboard | 89
Linus Torvalds   | Monitor stand       | 39.5

blocks.text: A view stores the *query*, not the result: every time you select from it, the underlying tables are read, so it always reflects the current data and takes no extra space. (PostgreSQL and Oracle also offer *materialized* views that do store results and must be refreshed.) Aggregating over a view is common:

blocks.code:
CREATE VIEW order_details AS
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, o.quantity,
       ROUND(p.price * o.quantity, 2) AS line_total, o.ordered_on
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id;
SELECT customer, ROUND(SUM(line_total), 2) AS spent
FROM order_details
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY spent DESC;

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE VIEW order_details AS

customer          | spent
------------------+------
Ada Lovelace      | 102.5
Guido van Rossum  | 89
Linus Torvalds    | 57.48
Grace Hopper      | 28.5
Margaret Hamilton | 27.5

blocks.text: Because every playground run starts from a fresh database, each example recreates the view; in a real database you create it once. `DROP VIEW order_details` removes it. Simple single-table views are updatable in PostgreSQL and MySQL; SQLite views are always read-only, and inserting into one fails with *cannot modify ... because it is a view*.

Without an index, `WHERE customer_id = 2` makes the database read every row of `orders` (a *scan*). An index on `customer_id` keeps the values sorted with pointers to their rows, so the database can *search* directly. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` (SQLite; `EXPLAIN` in PostgreSQL and MySQL) shows which strategy will be used:

blocks.content:
id | parent | notused | detail
---+--------+---------+------------
2  | 0      | 216     | SCAN orders

OK: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id)

id | parent | notused | detail
---+--------+---------+--------------------------------------------------------------
3  | 0      | 61      | SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_customer (customer_id=?)

blocks.text: Before the index the plan says `SCAN orders`; after it, `SEARCH orders USING INDEX`. The numeric columns are internal identifiers; the `detail` column is what to read. On 8 rows the difference is invisible, on 8 million it is the difference between milliseconds and minutes.

items: Columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN ... ON` and `ORDER BY` of frequent queries; foreign key columns such as `orders.customer_id` are the classic candidates.
Primary keys are indexed automatically, and a `UNIQUE` constraint creates an index as well.
A composite index on `(country, joined)` serves queries on `country` alone and on both columns, but not on `joined` alone: column order matters.
A `UNIQUE INDEX` enforces uniqueness just like the constraint, as the next example shows.

blocks.code:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_customers_name ON customers (name);
INSERT INTO customers (name, country, joined) VALUES ('Ada Lovelace', 'UK', '2025-09-01');

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_customers_name ON customers (name)
UNIQUE constraint failed: customers.name — in: INSERT INTO customers (name, country, joined) VALUES ('Ada Lovelace', 'UK', '202

blocks.title: Indexes are not free
blocks.text: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update each index on the table, and indexes take disk space. Indexing every column slows writes down for no gain. Also, an index on `email` does not help `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...`: applying a function to the column hides it from the index. Store the value in the form you search for, or create an index on the expression (SQLite and PostgreSQL support that).
Indexes appear in `sqlite_master` like tables, and `DROP INDEX` removes one without touching the data:

blocks.content:
OK: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id)
OK: CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products (category)

name                  | tbl_name
----------------------+---------
idx_orders_customer   | orders
idx_products_category | products

OK: DROP INDEX idx_products_category

name                | tbl_name
--------------------+---------
idx_orders_customer | orders

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Select from the `electronics` view, then create an index on `products(category)` and run the EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN line again to see SCAN turn into SEARCH.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: Selecting from a view re-runs its query against the current table data.
questions.explanation: A view is a stored query, so it always reflects the latest rows. Only materialized views keep a copy of the result.

questions.question: Which statement about indexes is correct?
questions.explanation: An index makes lookups on the indexed column fast but must be maintained on every write, so it slows inserts, updates and deletes slightly.
options: They speed up lookups but slow down writes
They store a copy of the whole table

seo.title: SQL Views and Indexes – Reusable Queries, Faster Lookups
seo.description: Learn SQL views and indexes: save a query as a view, create indexes on filter and join columns, check them with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and weigh their write cost.
